theory.overview: Individual cryptographic primitives—ciphers, hashes, MACs, signatures—are building blocks. Real security requires protocols that combine these correctly to achieve specific goals. The Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol, securing every HTTPS connection, exemplifies this: it negotiates algorithms, authenticates servers, establishes session keys, and protects data in transit. Understanding protocols matters because subtle flaws—incorrect message ordering, missing authentication, or improper nonce handling—lead to devastating attacks. From the BEAST attack on TLS 1.0 to Heartbleed in OpenSSL, protocol vulnerabilities have shaped internet security. This chapter examines how protocols compose primitives and the principles that distinguish secure protocols from broken ones.

sections.title: TLS Handshake Overview
sections.content: The TLS handshake establishes secure communication in several phases. First, the ClientHello proposes protocol versions and cipher suites; ServerHello responds with its choices and sends its certificate chain. The client verifies the server certificate against trusted CAs. Both parties perform key exchange (usually ECDHE for forward secrecy), generating pre-master secrets. They derive session keys from the pre-master secret using HKDF. Finally, they exchange Finished messages—encrypted and MAC'd using the new session keys—proving the handshake succeeded. This produces two sets of keys: client-to-server and server-to-client, each with separate encryption and MAC keys. The entire handshake is authenticated, preventing downgrade and man-in-the-middle attacks.

sections.title: Protocol Attacks and Defenses
sections.content: Protocol history reveals recurring vulnerability patterns. Downgrade attacks force clients to use weak protocol versions; TLS 1.3 prevents this by encoding supported versions in the ServerHello's random nonce. Replay attacks resend captured messages; nonces and sequence numbers prevent this. Padding oracle attacks exploit error message differences in CBC mode; constant-time decryption and TLS 1.3's AEAD-only design eliminate this. Certificate mis-issuance has enabled attackers to get valid certs for domains they don't own; Certificate Transparency logs now mandate public logging of all certificates. Understanding these attacks teaches the adversarial mindset required for protocol design.
keyPoints: Downgrade attacks: prevented by version enforcement
Padding oracles: prevented by constant-time operations

sections.title: Perfect Forward Secrecy in Practice
sections.content: Without forward secrecy, capturing encrypted traffic and later stealing the server's private key enables retroactive decryption. Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE or ECDHE) prevents this by generating temporary key pairs for each session. The server's long-term key (RSA or ECDSA) only authenticates the ephemeral DH public key. After the session, ephemeral private keys are discarded. Even if the server's certificate key is compromised later, past session keys cannot be recovered because the ephemeral DH private keys are gone. TLS 1.3 mandates forward secrecy—static RSA key transport is no longer allowed. This protects historical traffic even against future key compromises.
keyPoints: Static key transport: vulnerable to retroactive decryption
Ephemeral DH: new keys per session
Protects past sessions from future key theft

sections.title: Protocol Design Principles
sections.content: Secure protocol design follows established principles. Minimize attack surface: TLS 1.3 removed obsolete cipher suites and features, reducing complexity. Fail securely: any error should terminate the connection rather than continue with degraded security. Explicit authentication: every message should be authenticated, either implicitly (within encrypted record) or explicitly (signed). Defense in depth: multiple redundant protections so single failures don't compromise security. Clear specification: ambiguities lead to implementation divergences and vulnerabilities. Cryptographic agility: ability to update algorithms without protocol changes. These principles guide not just TLS but all secure protocol development, from messaging apps to blockchain consensus.
keyPoints: Minimize attack surface: remove obsolete features
Fail secure: terminate on any error

steps.title: ClientHello
steps.description: Client proposes TLS version, cipher suites, and sends random nonce.

steps.title: ServerHello
steps.description: Server selects version and cipher, sends its certificate chain.

steps.title: Certificate Verification
steps.description: Client verifies server certificate against trusted CAs, checks validity and hostname.

steps.title: Key Exchange
steps.description: Server and client perform ephemeral DH key exchange, generating shared secret.

steps.title: Key Derivation
steps.description: Derive session keys from shared secret using HKDF.

steps.title: Finished Messages
steps.description: Both sides send Finished message encrypted with new keys, verifying handshake integrity.

steps.title: Application Data
steps.description: Secure channel established. Application data encrypted with session keys.

practiceProblems.title: TLS 1.3 vs 1.2
practiceProblems.description: What is a major improvement of TLS 1.3 over TLS 1.2?

solution.answer: TLS 1.3 reduces handshake to 1-RTT, mandates forward secrecy, and removes obsolete cipher suites
solution.explanation: TLS 1.3 is faster (fewer round trips), more secure (mandates PFS, removes static RSA), and simpler (removed legacy algorithms like MD5, SHA-1, and RSA key exchange).

practiceProblems.title: Certificate Purpose
practiceProblems.description: What role do certificates play in the TLS handshake?
hints: Certificates bind identity to public key

solution.answer: Certificates authenticate the server's identity and provide their public key
solution.explanation: The server's certificate proves its identity (hostname) and contains its public key. It's signed by a Certificate Authority that the client trusts. This prevents man-in-the-middle attacks by ensuring the client talks to the real server.

practiceProblems.title: Downgrade Attack
practiceProblems.description: How does a man-in-the-middle force TLS clients to use weaker protocol versions?
hints: Client falls back to weaker option

solution.answer: By intercepting and modifying ClientHello to remove strong options, forcing the server to choose a weaker protocol
solution.explanation: In a downgrade attack, the MITM intercepts the ClientHello and removes modern protocol versions and cipher suites. The server, seeing only legacy options, negotiates a weaker connection. TLS 1.3 prevents this by including supported versions in the ServerHello's random field.

practiceProblems.title: 0-RTT Resumption
practiceProblems.description: What is the trade-off of TLS 1.3's 0-RTT session resumption?
hints: Uses pre-shared key from previous session
No forward secrecy for early data

solution.answer: 0-RTT improves performance but lacks forward secrecy for the initial data and is vulnerable to replay attacks
solution.explanation: 0-RTT allows sending data with the ClientHello, saving a round trip. However, it uses a pre-shared key from the previous session, so if that key is compromised, the 0-RTT data can be decrypted. It also requires replay protection mechanisms since 0-RTT data can be replayed by attackers.

practiceProblems.title: Certificate Transparency
practiceProblems.description: How does Certificate Transparency prevent rogue CA certificate issuance?
hints: All certificates must be logged publicly
Domain owners can monitor for misissuance

solution.answer: By requiring all certificates to be publicly logged, making it impossible for rogue certificates to remain hidden
solution.explanation: Certificate Transparency requires CAs to log every issued certificate to public, append-only logs before browsers accept them. Domain owners can monitor these logs for certificates issued for their domains without authorization, detecting rogue CA behavior quickly.

snippets.title: TLS Connection with Python
snippets.code:
import ssl
import socket

# Create SSL context with TLS 1.3
context = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_CLIENT)
context.minimum_version = ssl.TLSVersion.TLSv1_3
context.load_verify_locations('/path/to/ca-bundle.crt')

# Connect to server
with socket.create_connection(('example.com', 443)) as sock:
    with context.wrap_socket(sock, server_hostname='example.com') as tls_sock:
        print(f"TLS version: {tls_sock.version()}")
        print(f"Cipher: {tls_sock.cipher()}")
        print(f"Certificate: {tls_sock.getpeercert()}")
        
        # Send HTTP request
        tls_sock.send(b'GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: example.com\r\n\r\n')
        response = tls_sock.recv(4096)
        print(response.decode())
